sections.abstract: Aims: To search for novel Vip3A proteins for controlling insect pests. Methods and Results: A pair of universal primers was designed based on the conserved regions of five vip3A genes. Amplified products were digested with the HindIII and EcoR enzymes so as to confirm different restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) patterns used to identify vip3A-type genes. The vip3A gene types of 606 Bacillus thuringiensis strains were screened and three patterns of RFLP were successfully identified. Two novel vip3A genes were found and one of these, vip3Aa19, was further characterized and its product was confirmed toxic to Spodoptera exigua, Helicoverpa armigera and Plutella xylostella larvae. Partial sequences of another novel vip3A-type gene were obtained that shared 83% homology with that of the vip3Af1 gene. Conclusions: A polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-RFLP system we developed could be used for identifying novel vip3A-genes from B. thuringiensis strains. A novel Vip3A protein was found to have a broader insecticidal spectrum. Significance and Impact of the Study: The reported method is a powerful tool to find novel Vip3A proteins from large-scale B. thuringiensis strains. The novel Vip3A protein may be used to control insect pests or resistant insect pests by constructing genetically engineered strains or transgenic plants.
sections.introduction: Bacillus thuringiensis, a gram-positive bacterium, produces crystalline inclusions during sporulation. The insecticidal activity of B. thuringiensis is, in large part, associated with its ability to synthesize a crystalline parasporal inclusion body containing highly specific insecticidal proteins known as Cry and Cyt proteins (Schnepf et al. 1998). A number of extracellular compounds, in addition to crystal-associated toxin polypeptides, may contribute to the virulence of B. thuringiensis, including d-exotoxins, phospholipases, proteases, chitinases and secreted vegetative insecticidal proteins (Vip) (Schnepf et al. 1998;Donovan et al. 2001;Bhalla et al. 2005). Vip bear no similarity to d-endotoxins and have been shown to have a broad insecticidal spectrum, which includes activity against a wide variety of lepidopteran (Estruch et al. 1996;Selvapandiyan et al. 2001;Doss et al. 2002;Mesrati et al. 2005) as well as coleopteran pests (Estruch et al. 1996). Recently, the B. thuringiensis nomenclature committee proposed a classification in which all VVip-related sequences cloned were classified into three different families (Vip1, Vip2 and Vip3). Vip3-type proteins were categorized within two classes (Vip3A and Vip3B) and nine subclasses (Vip3Aa to Vip3Ag and Vip3Ba to Vip3Bb) (Crickmore et al. 2006). To date, 44 vip-type genes have been cloned, including 28 kinds of vip3-type genes (26 kinds of Vip3A and two kinds of Vip3B) (Crickmore et al. 2006). The vip3A gene encodes an 88-kDa protein that is secreted into the supernatant by B. thuringiensis cultures (Estruch et al. 1996) and Vip3A proteins have a wide spectrum (Yu et al. 1997;Doss et al. 2002;Lee et al. 2003). Mesrati et al. (2005) reported that the vip3A gene was carried by the large plasmid (Mesrati et al. 2005). Vip3A protein can bind to brush border membrane vesicles (BBMV) (Lee et al. 2003), and competition binding assays demonstrated that Vip3A does not inhibit the binding of either Cry1Ac or Cry2Ab2 and vice versa (Lee et al. 2006). Active Vip3A proteins formed stable ion channels in the absence of any reporters, supporting pore formation as an inherent property of Vip3A (Lee et al. 2003). It has also been demonstrated that Vip3A proteins have unique insecticidal mechanisms of action that are distinct from Cry proteins in what pertains to receptor binding and ion channel properties (Lee et al. 2003(Lee et al. , 2006)). These factors highlight the potential benefits of the use of Vip3A in insecticide resistance management strategies (Lee et al. 2006). Given the wide spectrum and different modes of insecticidal action from cry genes, the novel vip3A genes that are obtained from B. thuringiensis strains could potentially be very useful as a biological control agent against insensitive or resistant insect pests. A variety of polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based methods have been developed to detect different cry genes from B. thuringiensis strains (Ceron et al. 1995;Ben-Dov et al. 1999;Song et al. 2003). Ce¢cile et al. (2005) had described the identification of novel vip3 genes by PCR amplification using primers specific to conserved regions followed by restriction mapping of the PCR product. The present study reported the large-scale use of PCR-restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) to identify vip3A-type genes from B. thuringiensis strains. Both known and novel vip3A genes can be identified, as our method utilizes a new pair of universal primers that were designed based on the conserved regions of five vip3A-type genes. In the current study, two novel vip3A-type genes from B. thuringiensis strains were identified, and one was further characterized. Additionally, we demonstrate that the novel Vip3Aa protein was active against cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera), beet armyworm (Spodoptera exigua) and Plutella xylostella. The B. thuringiensis nomenclature committee designated this protein as Vip3Aa19. ## Bacterial strains and plasmids A total of 606 B. thuringiensis isolates were obtained from the B. thuringiensis R&D Center of the Hubei Academy of Agricultural Sciences, the Bacterial Stock Center of the Chinese Academy of Forestry Sciences and the Department of Plant Protection of Northeast Agriculture University, Harbin, China. Vector pET-21b (+) and Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) were purchased from Novagen Co. (Madison, WI, USA). ## Chemical reagents and enzymes Chemical reagents were purchased from Promega Biosciences, Inc. (Madison). KOD plus DNA polymerase and Taq DNA polymerase were purchased from Toyobo Biotech Co. Ltd. (Tokyo, Japan). Restriction enzymes were obtained from New England Biolabs, Inc. (Beverly, MA, USA). ## Template preparation and PCR-RFLP Bacillus thuringiensis strains were incubated (30ºC, overnight with shaking at 220 rev min )1 ) in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium containing 1% tryptone, 0AE5% yeast extract, 1% NaCl; pH 7AE0 and subsequently centrifuged. A sample of the incubation culture medium was collected (1 ml) and the pellet was resuspended in 200 ll of purified water, boiled (7AE5 min), centrifuged (12 235 g, 2 min) and the soluble fraction was collected as a template for PCR amplification. From a PC Gene multi-alignment analysis, a part of the conserved regions from five published vip3A-type genes (vip3Aa1, vip3Ab1, vip3Ad2, vip3Ae1 and vip3Af1) was located. A pair of universal primers (Svip3-Svip5) was designed. The sequences of oligonucleotide primers Svip3 and Svip5 are complementary. The sequences of the oligonucleotide primers and the alignments of five published vip3A-type gene sequences are shown in Table 1. The mismatch of the oligonucleotide primers among those sequences is less than four nucleotides (Table 1). The PCR mixture (50 ll) contained 1 ll of templates with reaction buffer, deoxynucleoside triphosphate (250 lmol l )1 ), primer (0AE2 lmol l )1 ) and Taq DNA polymerase (1 U). PCR was carried out for 30 cycles (94°C, 1 min; 53°C, 1 min; 72°C, 3 min) and PCR products were digested with both Hind and EcoRI enzymes. Restriction fragments were separated in 1AE5% agarose gels. Table 1 shows the predicted fragment sizes of PCR products for five kinds of known vip3A genes as well as the two novel vip3A-type genes identified in this study. KOD plus DNA polymerase (1 U; Toyobo Biotech Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) amplified the template of Bt41 with primers Svip3-Svip5. The PCR mixture (50 ll) contained 500 ng of plasmid, primer (200 pmol l )1 ), 10 mmol l )1 of dNTP mixture (1 ll), 50 mmol l )1 of MgCl 2 solution (1 ll) and KOD plus DNA polymerase. PCR was carried out for 30 cycles (94°C, 1 min; 53°C, 1 min; 68°C, 3 min). The PCR product was extension (10 min, 72°C) by Taq DNA polymerase and then cloned into a pMD18-T vector (Toyobo Biotech Co., Ltd.). The PCR was repeated thrice and three different clones were sequenced by Sangon Co. (Shanghai, China). ## Cloning of a vip3A gene from BtAL Based on the published Vip3 sequences in Genbank, according to their sequence homology of the N-and C-termini was a pair of primers (VIP3-VIP5) designed which contained an NdeI site at the 5¢end and a SalI site at the 3¢ end. The full-length vip3A-type gene containing an NdeI site at the 5¢end and a SalI site at the 3¢ end was obtained by PCR amplification from the BtAL strain with the sense primer VIP5 (5¢-GGAATTCCATATGAACAA-GAATAATACTAAATTAAGC-3¢) and the reverse primer VIP3 (5¢-ACGCGTCGACTACTTAATAGAGACATCG-TAAAAATG-3¢). PCR was performed with a 50-ll (final volume) mixture containing 500 ng of plasmid, primer (200 pmol l )1 ), 10 mmol l )1 dNTP mixture (1 ll), 50 mmol l )1 MgCl 2 solution (1 ll) and KOD plus DNA polymerase. PCR conditions were as follows: initial denaturation (94°C, 4 min), 30 amplification cycles (1 min, 94°C; 1 min, 53°C; 3 min, 68°C) and extension (10 min, 68°C). The PCR product was inserted into a pET-21b vector with NdeI and SalI sites and transformed into E. coli BL21 (DE3). Three clones of PCR products repeated thrice were sequenced by Sangon Co. (Shanghai) and analysed by Vector NTI Suite 9 (Informax, Frederick, MD). ## vip3A gene expression and protein analysis Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) harbouring the cloned vip3Aa gene was grown in LB medium with ampicillin (100 g ml )1 , overnight) then inoculated at a 1% concentration into fresh LB medium (1000 ml) containing the ampicillin (100 g ml )1 ). Cultures were incubated with shaking (37°C, 250 rev min )1 ) until an optical density (OD) of 0AE6-0AE8 was reached (measured at 600 nm), after which isopropyl-b-d-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) was added to a final concentration of 0AE5 mmol l )1 . Cultures were maintained with shaking (18°C, 18 h, 130 rev min )1 ) then centrifuged (12 235 g, 10 min, 4ºC). The culture supernatant was discarded, and then the sediments were resuspended in 10 mmol l )1 of Tris-HCL (pH 8AE0), sonicate (medium-intensity pulses, 10 min) centrifuged again (12 235 g, 10 min, 4ºC) and the pellet and soluble fraction were collected. Furthermore, the pellet was resuspended in the same volume as the recovered supernatant. Sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoretic (SDS-PAGE) analysis utilized the method described by Sambrook et al. (1989). Protein content analysis of the soluble fraction was estimated utilizing the Bradford (1976). The vip3Aa11 gene was cloned by our laboratory and transformed into E. coli BL21 (DE3) (Liu et al. 2004). Vip3Aa11 protein was obtained according to the reference (Liu et al. 2004). ## Insecticidal activity Insecticidal activity against first-instar larvae of Asian corn borer (Ostrinia furnacalis), cotton bollworm (H. armigera) and beet armyworm (S. exigua) were measured by incorporating a suspension containing different serial dilutions of soluble fraction protein into the artificial diet. The Vip3Aa19 and Vip3Aa11 protein were tested side-by-side. Toxicity studies on P. xylostella larvae (second-instar larvae) were conducted on fresh leaf discs by leaf dip bioassays (Tabashnik et al. 1993). Discs cut from cabbage (grown in the greenhouse) leaves were used for P. xylostella. A total of 24 larvae were each given an artificial diet [Asian corn borer (O. furnacalis), cotton bollworm (H. armigera) and beet armyworm (S. exigua)]. Additionally, 20 P. xylostella larvae were placed on a leaf disc and their fates were monitored after 4 days for P. xylostella and after 7 days for the other insects. Bioassays were repeated a minimum of three times and 50% lethal concentrations (LC 50 ) were calculated by Probit analysis (Finney 1971). ## Nucleotide sequence accession numbers The nucleotide sequence data of Vip3Aa19 were assigned GenBank accession numbers DQ241674 and DQ250256 for partial sequence of Vip3A obtained from Bt41. ## Identification of vip3A genes from Bacillus thuringiensis strains Vip3A genes were screened in 606 isolates by PCR-RFLP. A total of 382 strains harboured vip3A genes, based on a positive PCR signal. The vip3A-type genes of these strains were identified by fragment patterns of Hind and EcoRI digestion products. Agarose gel data confirmed that 315 isolates had a vip3Aa-type RFLP pattern (Fig. 1), with four main bands at 861, 255, 186 and 154 bp conforming to the predicted fragments of vip3Aa-type genes (Fig. 1; lanes 1 to 3, 7, 8, 13, 14 and 16). Of these strains, 52, including strain BtAL (Fig. 1, lane 5) showed a novel vip3A-type RFLP pattern, which had five main bands at 861, 255, 154, 147 and 39 bp (Fig. 1; lanes 4, 5, 9, 12 and 15). A second novel vip3A-type pattern, with three main bands at 1116, 186 and 154 bps was also identified in 15 isolates (Fig. 1; lanes 6, 10 and 11), including B. thuringiensis Bt41 (Fig. 1; lane 11). ## vip3A gene cloning and sequence analysis A partial vip3A gene of B. thuringiensis isolate Bt41 was obtained and sequenced. sections.discussion: To date, several PCR-based methods for cry gene identification have been developed (Ceron et al. 1995;Juarez-Perez et al. 1997;Ben-Dov et al. 1999;Song et al. 2003), including specific primer PCR, multiplex PCR, exclusive PCR and PCR-RFLP. These methods directly detect known cry genes from B. thuringiensis (Ceron et al. 1995;Ben-Dov et al. 1999) as well as identify novel cry genes (Juarez-Perez et al. 1997). In the current study, we reported the large-scale use of PCR-RFLP with a pair of novel universal primers to identify vip3A-type genes from B. thuringiensis strains. Our results indicated that vip3A gene was found in 382 B. thuringiensis among 606 strains. Estruch et al. (1996) previously reported that 60 strains contained vip3A-like genes among 463 B. thuringiensis isolates while Rice (1999) detected 29 strains that harboured vip3A-like genes from 128 B. thuringiensis isolates. These studies demonstrated that vip3A genes were distrib-uted widely in B. thuringiensis strains. It was very interesting that an unpredicted RFLP pattern of Bt41 different from that of the five known vip3A genes was found. We cloned and sequenced the PCR product of Bt41 with the primers (Svip3-Svip5). Sequence analysis showed that the PCR fragment shared the highest sequence homology (83%), among known vip3A-type genes, with the vip3Af1 (isp3a) gene, which suggested that B. thuringiensis Bt41 might contain a novel vip3A holotype gene. Given that primers (Svip3-Svip5) were designed based on the sequences of five vip3A-type genes, (vip3Aa, vip3Ab, vip3Ad, vip3Ae and vip3Af), some B. thuringiensis strains had no positive or weak signals by PCR amplification. This may have resulted from the mismatch of primers with vip3A genes of some B. thuringiensis strains or the lack of existence of vip3A genes in some strains. Sequence analysis showed that the vip3B gene (Ce¢cile et al. 2005) was not identified with this pair of primers, and emphasizes the need to design more appropriate primers better able to identify more vip genes. The vip3Aa19 gene was cloned from BtAL using primers VIP3 and VIP5. These were designed to be homologous to other Vip3 toxin genes. The primers encoded the first nine and last eight codons of the cloned vip3Aa19 gene. The exact sequence of these codons in the BtAL gene was not known. However, the expressed Vip3Aa19 protein was toxic to S. exigua, H. armigera and P. xylostella. Vip3Aa19 protein shared the highest sequence homology among Vip3Aa proteins (97%) with Vip3Aa11, with only 19 amino acid residues different between the Vip3Aa19 and Vip3Aa11 proteins (Table 3). Vip3Aa19 protein showed insecticidal activities against S. exigua, H. armigera, P. xylostella with little toxicity to O. furnacalis while Vip3Aa11 showed toxicity against S. exigua and H. armigera and low activity to P. xylostella, confirming they had a different insecticidal spectrum. There were 19 different amino acid residues between Vip3Aa19 and Vip3Aa11 toxins (Table 3). It was difficult to determine which amino acid residues among them were important for insecticidal activity against P. xylostella. Previous reports have also demonstrated that changes in several amino acid residues in other Vip3A proteins could affect protein insecticidal activity (Estruch et al. 1996;Selvapandiyan et al. 2001;Doss et al. 2002). Differences in only two residues (Q 284 K, E 742 G) between Vip3Aa9 and Vip3Aa1 proteins (Estruch et al. 1996;Selvapandiyan et al. 2001), and one residue (E 742 G) between Vip3Aa9 and Vip3Aa10 proteins (Selvapandiyan et al. 2001;Doss et al. 2002), caused Vip3Aa9 protein to be ineffective against Agrotis ipsilon while Vip3Aa1 and Vip3Aa10 proteins continued to be effective (Estruch et al. 1996;Doss et al. 2002). These results suggest that different regions of Vip3A protein may confer different insecticidal activities. Our finding of novel Vip3A protein, with different amino acid residues resulting in a broader insecticidal spectrum, may significantly contribute to control resistant insect pests.
